title: SiPearl delivers the first Rhea1 CPUs to Bull for integration into JUPITER, Europe’s fastest operating supercomputer
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

SiPearl’s delivery of the first Rhea1 processors to Bull for integration into JUPITER marks a transition from European semiconductor ambition to working hardware. JUPITER, hosted by the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Germany, is Europe’s first exascale system and its fastest operating supercomputer. Its architecture combines a GPU-accelerated Booster Module with a general-purpose Cluster Module. Rhea1 will power that cluster within Bull’s BullSequana XH3000 platform.

Rhea1 is a European-designed, high-performance processor created for supercomputing and artificial-intelligence workloads. It combines 80 Arm Neoverse V1 cores with high-bandwidth memory, DDR5 connectivity, and PCIe Gen5 interfaces. This design emphasizes memory bandwidth and energy efficiency, qualities needed for scientific applications that move enormous datasets rather than simply performing repeated calculations. Delivery begins the process of hardware validation, system integration, software optimization, and production deployment.

Why does this matter? First, it advances European technological sovereignty. Europe’s leading supercomputers have historically depended heavily on processors designed by American or Asian companies. Rhea1 gives Europe control over a strategically important part of the computing stack. Although the chips are manufactured by TSMC, European ownership of the design and intellectual property still reduces critical dependence.

Second, installation in JUPITER gives SiPearl a major reference customer. Successful operation would validate Rhea1 at scale, strengthen confidence among governments and commercial buyers, and support a European processor ecosystem of software developers, system builders, researchers, and suppliers.

Finally, the development expands JUPITER’s usefulness. Its heterogeneous design can match GPU-heavy workloads to the Booster while directing memory-intensive, general-purpose tasks to the Rhea1 cluster. That flexibility supports climate modelling, materials science, medicine, engineering, and AI.

The delivery is therefore more than a component shipment: it is a test of whether Europe can convert publicly backed research into secure, dependable, sovereign computing infrastructure. Its ultimate significance will depend on performance, reliability, software maturity, and timely deployment.
